INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
Prosecutors Against Gun Violence (“PAGV”) is an
independent, nonpartisan coalition that identifies
and advances prosecutorial and policy solutions to the
national crisis of gun violence.1  PAGV is composed of
fifty prosecutors, serving tens of millions of residents,
in jurisdictions spanning ne arly thirty states.  As
prosecutors, PAGV’s member s play a critical role in
protecting public safety, a paramount objective of
state and local government.  This mission includes
promoting best practices for prosecuting gun offenses,
defending commonsense gun restrictions, and
working with constituents to understand the best
means of enforcing existing laws.
PAGV Co-Chair Alvin L. Bragg is the District
Attorney of New York County (“DANY”).  DANY
enforces state and local criminal laws in Manhattan,
the most densely populated county in the country
with nearly 1.7 million residents.  Combatting gun
violence is DANY’s top priority. 2  DANY routinely
prosecutes defendants who use firearms to perpetrate
violent crimes, including murders, assaults, and
robberies.  Beyond criminal prosecutions, DANY also
devotes considerable resources to addressing the
underlying causes of violent crimes, a crucial

PAGV Co-Chair Zach Klein is the Columbus City
Attorney.  Among other responsibilities, his office
prosecutes criminal cases in the City of Columbus,
which is the largest city in Ohio.  Columbus has more
than 900,000 residents; it is the county seat for
Franklin County; and it is the State’s capital.  The
Columbus City Attorney’s Office prosecutes
misdemeanor offenses inside the City of Columbus,
including cases of domestic  violence as well as
weapons-under-disability charges.  In addition, the
Columbus City Attorney’s Office has been a leading
voice for commonsense gun regulations, including
suing the State of Ohio to force it to fix its background
check system; successfully  defending the city’s
weapons-under-disability law; and engaging in other
litigation efforts to overturn Ohio’s firearms
preemption law, which prohibits municipalities from
passing their own gun laws.
PAGV has a direct intere st in this litigation,
which considers whether the Constitution forbids
states—here, Connecticut and Illinois—from banning
assault weapons.  PAGV members enforce
comparable assault-weapon bans in New York,
California, Delaware, Massachusetts, Maryland, and
Washington.
The experience of PAGV and its members
confirms that assault weapons bans can help address
what has become an exceptionally dangerous threat
to members of the public and law-enforcement officers
throughout the United States.  PAGV thus urges this
Court to affirm the decisions of the Second and

3

Seventh Circuits upholding Connecticut’s and
Illinois’s assault weapons bans.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Second Amendment does not entitle civilians
to carry firearms that are designed for military
combat.  AR-15 rifles easily fall into that category.
Marketed as the “civilian ve rsion” of the M-16, the
AR-15 differs from the M-16 in  that it fires only in
semiautomatic mode, whereas the M-16 can fire in
either semiautomatic or automatic mode. 3  Staples v.
United States , 511 U.S. 600, 603 (1994).  That
difference does not change the fact that AR-15s are
designed for military combat.  Indeed, rapid
semiautomatic fire—i.e., shooting a bullet every one
or two seconds—is generally considered to be more
deadly than automatic fire because a shooter can be
more precise and can also conserve ammunition,
while still outputting an enormous number of lifethreatening rounds.  Like the M-16, the AR-15
typically comes equipped with a number of features
that render it optimal for rapid semiautomatic fire.
And rifles optimized for rapid semiautomatic fire are
unusually dangerous because they level the playing
field between amateur gunmen and trained lawenforcement officers.  Unsurprisingly, the availability
of semiautomatic AR-15 rifles has enabled lone
gunmen to overpower trained law-enforcement
officers and armed security guards.  And AR-15s are
also unusually dangerous because their capacity for
rapid semiautomatic fire enables gunmen to kill
people so quickly and precisely that it is often

3 Semiautomatic fire discharges “only one shot with a single
pull of the trigger.”  Staples, 511 U.S. at 602 n.1.  Automatic fire
discharges shots “repeatedly with each pull of the trigger.”  Id.

4

impossible for police to prevent large numbers of
casualties, even when officers arrive on the scene
immediately after a shooting starts.
ARGUMENT
AR-15 RIFLES ARE UNUSUALLY DANGEROUS
MILITARY WEAPONS, AND THE THREAT
THAT THEY POSE TO POLICE AND CIVILIANS
IS EXCEPTIONALLY DIFFICULT TO MANAGE
In District of Columbia v. Heller , this Court
recognized the historical tradition of banning
“dangerous and unusual weapons,” including “M-16
rifles” and similar guns that are “most useful in
military service.”  554 U. S. 570, 627 (2008).  AR-15
rifles fall into that category because like M-16s—and
unlike other semiautomatic guns—they are designed
to deliver rapid semiautomatic fire, which is the most
effective firing technique in modern military combat.
Moreover, because the sheer volume of fire that AR-
15s produce changes the dynamics of police-criminal
confrontations, these guns raise “unprecedented
societal concerns” and pose “regulatory challenges”
that “are not [] the same as those that preoccupied the
Founders in 1791 or the Reconstruction generation in
1868.”  New York State Rifle & Pi stol Ass’n, Inc. v.
Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 27 (2022).
A. AR-15s are designed to perform the most
effective firing technique in modern
military combat.
AR-15s share the core design features that make
M-16s most useful in military service.  See Heller, 554
U.S. at 627.  As this Court has recognized, the AR-15
is simply a semiautomatic-only version of the M-16,
which can deliver both semiautomatic and automatic

5

fire.  Staples, 511 U.S. at 603.  However, the
semiautomatic version of the rifle is still, by any
reasonable measure, designed for military use.
According to the U.S. Army, the “most important”
firing technique in modern military combat is “rapid
semiautomatic fire,” which is performed most
effectively when the soldier fires a bullet every one to
two seconds, or approximately 45 rounds per minute.
U.S. Dep’t of the Army,  Field Manual 3-22.9: Rifle
Marksmanship: M16-/M4-Series Weapons  at 2-1, 7-
12, 7-15 (2011 ed.) (“Army Field Manual”); U.S. Dep’t
of the Army,  Training Circular 3-22.9: Rifle and
Carbine at 8-19 (2016) (“Training Circular”).4
Like M-16s, AR-15s are designed to deliver rapid
semiautomatic fire.  To start, AR-15s and M-16s have
“identical rates” of semiau tomatic fire.  E. Gregory
Wallace, “Assault Weapon” Lethality, 88 Tenn. L. Rev.
1, 21 (2020).  Moreover , unlike other semiautomatic
guns, AR-15s typically include three core features
that make M-16s suitable for rapid semiautomatic
fire:  a pistol grip, a forward grip or barrel shroud, and
a detachable magazine.5  A pistol grip “helps manage
recoil during rapid or controlled fire.”6  A forward grip
or barrel shroud also helps manage recoil because it

Assault Weapons—What Are They? What’s So Bad About Them?
at 5–8 (May 2003), avail able at https://vpc.org/wpcontent/uploads/2025/07/bullethoses.pdf (accessed on Sept. 24,

6 Para Bellum Arms, AR Pistol Grip Design and Selection
Guide, available at https://pb-arms.com/design/pistol-grips/

6

enables the shooter “to hold the gun with the nontrigger hand, even though the barrel gets extremely
hot from firing multiple rounds.” 7  D e t a c h a b l e
magazines “allow shooters to reload and fire bullets
more quickly.”8  Unsurprisingly, then, in many tragic
incidents, shooters have used AR-15s and similar
assault weapons to deliver rates of fire that meet,  or
even exceed, the Army’s threshold for rapid
semiautomatic fire.  See Wallace, supra, at 22–23
(2019 Dayton, Ohio nightclub shooter fired 1.4 shots
per second; 2016 Orlando, Florida nightclub shooter
fired 2.7 shots per second; 2012 Aurora, Colorado
movie theater shooter fired “slightly more than one
shot per second”).
The capacity of AR-15 rifles to deliver rapid
semiautomatic fire confirms their status as unusually
dangerous military weapons.  After all, rapid
semiautomatic fire is the “most accurate” means for
placing “a large volume of fire” on multiple targets,
moving targets, or short-exposure targets, i.e., those
that quickly appear and disappear.  Army Field
Manual at 7-12, 7-32.  That  is important because,
under the stressful and fast-moving conditions of
modern military combat, placing a large volume of fire
on the target area is ofte n the most effective way to
“increase the probability of hitting the enemy.”
Thomas L. McNaugher, Marksmanship, McNamara
and the M16 Rifle: Organi zations, Analysis and

7 Violence Policy Center, Bullet Hoses, supra note 5, at 5
(quotation omitted).
8 Lucas Brady Woods, Colorado is poised to pass some of the
toughest gun laws in the country, NPR (Mar. 26, 2025), available
at https://www.npr.org/2025/03/26/nx-s1-5335549/colorado-gundetachable-magazines (accessed on Sept. 22, 2026).

7

Weapons Acquisition, THE RAND CORPORATION, at 22–
23 (1979).  Rapid semiautomatic fire is also the “most
accurate” technique for delivering “suppressive fire,”
which is used, among other things, to “prevent [the
enemy] from observing th e battlefield, effectively
using his weapons, or moving.”  Army Field Manual
at 7-15, 7-53.
The AR-15’s inability to deliver fully automatic
fire does not negate its status as an unusually
dangerous military weapon.  Indeed, automatic fire
has less military utility than rapid semiautomatic
fire.  Although there are some specific battlefield
scenarios in which automatic fire can be more
effective than rapid semiautomatic fire, the Army
Field Manual advises soldiers that M-16s “should
normally be employed in the semiautomatic fire
mode”—meaning that the recommended military use
for M-16s coincides with the AR-15’s design.  Army
Field Manual at 7-34. 9  Automatic fire is less deadly
than rapid semiautomatic fire for these two reasons:
first, automatic fire is “inherently less accurate”
because it generates more recoil per shot, id. at 7-32;
and second, automatic fire consumes ammunition
more quickly, see id. at 7-15.  By contrast, rapid
semiautomatic fire allows a gunman to output an
enormous number of rounds more accurately and
efficiently.  Accordingly, a gunman who fires an AR-

9 The Army Field Manual “has since been replaced with an
updated version, which again emphasizes the drawbacks of
automatic fire, noting that ‘[a]utomatic or burst fires drastically
decrease the probability of hit due to the rapid succession of

Gun Rights v. Lamont , 153 F.4th 213, 241 n.28 (2d Cir. 2025)
(quoting Training Circular § 8-21).

8

15 rifle at a police officer poses effectively the same
threat as he would if he were carrying an M-16.
B. AR-15s enable solo amateur shooters to
pose a grave and unmanageable threat
to police and civilian victims.
AR-15 rifles, which are designed to deliver rapid
semiautomatic fire, pose a novel regulatory challenge
that the Founders could not have foreseen.  See
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27.  Assaul t rifles such as AR-15s
enable criminals to inflict unprecedented harms
because these guns serve as an “equalizer” between
amateur marksmen and trained professionals.  C. J.
Chivers, The Gun  at 9 (2010).  Although the Army
traditionally believed in the primary importance of
“aimed fire,” its adoption of the M-16 assault rifle in
the late 1950s reflected its conclusion that, due to the
stressful and fast-moving conditions of modern
combat, “it was unlikely that in warfare the Army’s
best marksman would do any better than its worst at
hitting targets,” which meant that marksmanship
had become less important than delivering a large
volume of fire.  McNaugher, supra, at 4, 22–23
(emphasis in original).  Because rapid semiautomatic
fire is the most effective means for accurately
delivering a large volume of  fire in most combat
scenarios,  AR-15s can have the same equalizing
effect as other assault rifles.  Indeed, amici’s
experience confirms that AR-15s and other
semiautomatic assault weapons have enabled
amateur shooters to inflict unprecedented harms on
trained police officers and unarmed civilians.

9

1. AR-15s enable amateur shooters to
outgun trained police officers and
armed security guards.
AR-15s are designed for th e military tactics that
enable lone gunmen to overpower armed security
guards and repel police responders.  Faced with these
guns, security guards and policemen confront a threat
that has posed a serious challenge even to the
military.  During the Vietnam War, a “single guerilla”
armed with an assault rifle could slow the advance of
an entire company of U.S. soldiers.  Chivers, supra, at
9.  There are many tragic  examples demonstrating
the unprecedented disruption to social order that
occurs when lone gunmen use semiautomatic assault
rifles to deploy military firepower against security
guards and police officers:
x On July 28, 2025, in Manhattan, New York, a
lone gunman armed with an M4 semiautomatic
assault rifle walked into an office building and
gunned down a uniformed police officer, who
was working in the building as a security
guard, killing him.  The gunman then shot and
killed one more security guard and one civilian
before he gained access to the upper floors of
the building, where he killed another civilian.10
x On May 14, 2022, in Buffalo, New York, a
retired police officer who was working as a
security guard at a grocery store died when he

These examples illustrate one of the core
rationales behind the historical tradition supporting
a state’s choice to ban unusually dangerous weapons
such as M-16s and similar gu ns that are most useful
in military service.  See Heller, 554 U.S. at 627.  The
availability of military assault rifles such as AR-15s,
which are designed to perform the most effective
firing technique in modern military combat,
undermines the ability of police to protect themselves
and secure their own communities.  That is only
partly because police carrying handguns face a
serious disadvantage in firepower when they confront
gunmen armed with AR-15s.  Even when police also

the playing field between trained marksman and
amateur shooters can undermine the advantage that
the police would normally accrue from their
professional training.  Thus, for shootings that
involve assault weapons, police response plans often
“rely heavily” on an officer’s mental preparedness “to
run at gunfire . . . without adequate protection.”
